title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
directAnswer: Post-order DFS where each node returns the best single downward gain it can contribute to its parent — `node.val + max(0, leftGain, rightGain)` using only ONE child. Separately, at every node, consider the best path that bends through it (`node.val + leftGain + rightGain`, using BOTH children) and update a global maximum. The two distinct quantities — what you return up vs what you record globally — are the crux. O(n) time, O(h) space.

remember.pattern: Post-order DFS returning a partial value while tracking a global best (split at node)
remember.formula:
self.best = -inf
def gain(node):
    if not node: return 0
    left  = max(gain(node.left), 0)   # drop negative branches
    right = max(gain(node.right), 0)
    self.best = max(self.best, node.val + left + right)  # SPLIT through node
    return node.val + max(left, right)                   # return ONE side up
rules: A node **returns** `val + max(left, right)` (one branch) — a parent can only extend through a single child.
A node **updates the global** with `val + left + right` (both branches) — the apex of a path that bends here.
Clamp each child's gain at **max(gain, 0)** — a negative branch is better skipped than included.
Initialize the global best to **−∞**, not 0 — paths must contain at least one node and values can all be negative.
Use a **post-order** traversal: children's gains must be known before the parent computes anything.
whenToUse: Tree problems asking for an optimum over **paths/subtrees** where the answer can bend at a node
When the value returned to a parent differs from the value you want to record globally
Diameter-style problems: combine two child results at a node, return only one upward
Any 'best path' where including a negative contribution should be optional
antiSignals: Path must go root-to-leaf only → simpler top-down accumulation, no global split needed
You need the actual node sequence, not just the sum → carry/reconstruct the path, more bookkeeping
Graph with cycles, not a tree → DFS recursion no longer guarantees each node once
All values are non-negative AND any path allowed → still works, but the max(…,0) clamps never trigger
remember.takeaway: The defining trick is keeping two quantities apart: the *gain returned upward* uses a single child (so the parent can extend a straight path), while the *global best* allows a split through both children (a path that peaks at this node and can't go higher). This 'return partial, record full' shape is the same engine behind Diameter of Binary Tree and Longest Univalue Path.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can separate two related-but-different values in a single DFS: the best downward extension a node hands to its parent versus the best bending path that completes at that node — and whether you correctly drop negative contributions.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Returning `val + left + right` (the split sum) up to the parent, which lets a path use two branches of a node *and* still extend through it — an impossible path. Or initializing the answer to 0 and breaking on all-negative trees.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Articulate the two quantities precisely, justify the max(0, …) clamp, explain why post-order is required, and note the structural identity with Diameter of Binary Tree.

problemStatement:
A ***path*** in a binary tree is a sequence of nodes where each pair of adjacent nodes in the sequence has an edge connecting them. A node can only appear in the sequence ***at most once***. Note that the path does not need to pass through the root.

The ***path sum*** of a path is the sum of the node's values in the path.

Given the `root` of a binary tree, return ***the maximum path sum of any non-empty path***.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [1, 3 × 10⁴]
The path is non-empty (at least one node) and node values may be negative
understanding: We want the highest-sum path anywhere in the tree, where a path is any connected chain of nodes that visits each at most once and may bend at exactly one node (its highest point). It need not touch the root or reach a leaf. Because values can be negative, we may want to exclude entire branches.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the path have to pass through the root or reach a leaf?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. It can start and end anywhere, as long as the nodes form a connected chain. That's why we track a global maximum across all nodes.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can node values be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. So we clamp each child's contribution at 0 (skip negative branches) and initialize the answer to −∞, since even the best single node could be negative.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a path bend (go up through a node and back down)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, but only once — a path peaks at a single node where it may use both children. Above that node it can only continue through one side.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the path non-empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, at least one node. With all-negative values the answer is the single largest (least negative) node.

examples.explanation: The path 2 → 1 → 3 bends at the root and sums to 6.
The best path is 15 → 20 → 7 = 42; it bends at 20 and never touches the negative root.
Single node, all negative — the answer is that one node, which is why we start the global max at −∞.

diagrams.title: Two quantities at each node
diagrams.caption: Return one branch upward (so the parent can extend); record the both-branch split as a candidate global best.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Best Path Through Each Node
approaches.whenToMention: Useful to frame the problem ('every path peaks at some node') before showing how one DFS computes it all in O(n).
hints: Every path has a single highest node where it bends. Can you fix that node and ask: what's the best path peaking here?
For a fixed peak node, the best bending path is its value plus the best downward path into the left subtree plus the best downward path into the right subtree (each clamped at 0).
Computing 'best downward path from X' is itself a recursion. Doing it independently for every candidate peak repeats work — that's the O(n²).
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of the n possible peak nodes we compute the best downward path into each child, which is an O(n) DFS in the worst case → O(n²) time. Recursion depth is O(h).
approaches.explanation:
Start from the observation that *every* path peaks at exactly one node — the unique highest point where it may branch into both subtrees. So the global answer is the maximum, over all nodes, of 'best bending path that peaks at this node'.

**Best path peaking at a node.** Define `down(x)` = the largest sum of a straight downward path that starts at `x` and goes toward the leaves, taking 0 if every option is negative. Then the best path peaking at node `p` is `p.val + max(down(p.left), 0) + max(down(p.right), 0)`. Take the max of that across all nodes.

**Why it's quadratic.** Computing `down(x)` is itself a recursion over a subtree. If we call it independently for every peak candidate, we recompute the same downward sums over and over — n peaks × O(n) per `down` = O(n²).

**Why mention it.** It cleanly establishes the framing ('paths peak at a node; combine two downward arms') that the optimal solution reuses. The leap to O(n) is simply: compute each node's downward gain *once* and fold the peak check into the same traversal.
approaches.insight: The realization that every path has a single bend point converts a scary 'all paths' search into 'for each node, the best path that peaks here'. The only inefficiency is recomputing downward sums — memoizing them into one post-order pass is the whole optimization.

dryRun.intro: Try each node as the peak; best bending sum wins.

java.explanation: Best path that bends at root: its value plus both clamped downward arms.
Also consider paths peaking somewhere in the left subtree.
down(): best straight downward path; recomputed per peak → O(n²).

python.explanation: Best downward path from node; clamp at 0 to skip negative branches.
Both arms combined — the path that peaks at this node.
Max over this peak and peaks in either subtree; the repeated down() calls cause O(n²).

pitfalls: Recomputing down() for every peak — the source of the quadratic blow-up.
Returning 0 from the empty subtree but starting best at 0 — breaks all-negative trees.
Forgetting that the peak path uses BOTH arms while down() uses only one.

approaches.name: Single Post-Order DFS — Gain Up, Split Recorded (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. 'One DFS: each node returns its best single-branch gain; I update a global max with the two-branch split.'
hints: In the brute force, down(x) was recomputed everywhere. What if each node computed its downward gain exactly once and passed it up?
Have the recursion return the best downward gain (one branch). At the same node, while you have both children's gains, compute the bending path (both branches) and update a global best.
Clamp negative child gains to 0 so they're simply skipped. Return val + max(leftGain, rightGain) upward, but record val + leftGain + rightGain as a global candidate.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single post-order visit touches each node once with O(1) work → O(n) time. The only extra memory is the recursion stack, bounded by the tree height → O(h) space.
approaches.explanation:
Fold the whole computation into one post-order DFS. The key is to keep two related quantities strictly separate.

**Quantity 1 — the gain returned upward.** When the recursion finishes a node, it returns the maximum sum of a path that *starts at this node and goes straight down through at most one child*: `node.val + max(leftGain, rightGain)`. We return only one branch because the parent will attach this node as a link in a straight chain — a chain can't pass through both children of a node and still continue upward. We clamp each child's gain at `max(gain, 0)`: if a branch is negative, skipping it (contributing 0) is never worse.

**Quantity 2 — the global best (the split).** At the *same* node we also ask: what's the best path whose highest point is this node? Such a path may dip into both children, giving `node.val + leftGain + rightGain`. This value is *not* returned upward (a path can't both fork here and extend to the parent), but it's a candidate for the overall answer, so we fold it into a global maximum.

**Why these must differ.** This is the entire difficulty of the problem. If you returned the split sum (`val + left + right`) to the parent, the parent could attach a path that already used both of this node's branches and *still* extend upward — a shape that revisits the node, which paths forbid. Returning only the single best branch keeps every upward extension a legal straight chain, while the global captures the legal bends.

**Why post-order.** A node can't compute either quantity until it knows both children's gains, so we must finish the children before the parent — that's post-order (left, right, then node).

**Why −∞ initialization.** The path must be non-empty and values can all be negative, so the answer might be a single negative node. Starting the global at 0 would wrongly return 0 for `[-3]`. Initialize to −∞ (or to root.val) so the true maximum, however negative, survives.
approaches.insight: The pattern is 'return a partial result, record a complete result'. The upward return is deliberately weaker (one branch) than the value we score globally (two branches) because the two answer different questions: 'how can my parent use me?' versus 'what's the best path that ends with me at the top?'. This exact split powers Diameter of Binary Tree (return depth, record left+right) and Longest Univalue Path.

dryRun.intro: Post-order. Each node returns one-branch gain; global best records the two-branch split. best starts at −∞.

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
def maxPathSum(self, root: 'TreeNode') -> int:
    self.best = float('-inf')

    def gain(node: 'TreeNode') -> int:
        if node is None:
            return 0
        left_gain = max(gain(node.left), 0)
        right_gain = max(gain(node.right), 0)
        self.best = max(self.best, node.val + left_gain + right_gain)  # split
        return node.val + max(left_gain, right_gain)                   # one branch up

    gain(root)
    return self.best

java.explanation: Start at −∞ so an all-negative tree returns its least-negative node, not 0.
Clamp negative branches to 0 — skipping them never hurts.
Record the bending path peaking here (BOTH branches) as a global candidate.
Return only ONE branch so the parent extends a legal straight chain.

python.explanation: Non-empty path + possibly all-negative values ⇒ initialize below any real sum.
Negative downward gain is discarded (contribute 0 instead).
Two-branch split is the best path that peaks at this node — global only.
Hand the parent a single-branch gain; never the split.

diagrams.title: The winning bend at node 20
diagrams.caption: 15 → 20 → 7 = 42 peaks at 20; the negative root is excluded by the max(0, …) clamp.

edgeCases.behavior: Leaf: left=right=0, split = -3 → best = -3; returns -3. The −∞ start is what lets a negative answer win.
Child -1 clamped to 0 for the parent; best becomes max(-1, -2) = -1 — the single least-negative node.
Negative middle is clamped where it would hurt; the algorithm still finds the best contiguous bend or single node.

pitfalls: Returning val + leftGain + rightGain upward — allows an illegal path that forks and still extends.
Initializing best to 0 — wrong on all-negative trees (returns 0 instead of a negative node).
Forgetting the max(0, gain) clamp — a negative branch then drags the sum down instead of being skipped.

commonMistakes: Returning the two-branch split sum to the parent instead of the single-branch gain.
Initializing the global maximum to 0 rather than −∞, breaking all-negative trees.
Not clamping negative child gains to 0, so harmful branches are forced into the path.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Returning the split sum upward
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The value handed to the parent must be a straight downward chain (one child). Returning val + left + right lets the parent extend a path that already used both of this node's branches — a shape that would revisit the node, which paths forbid.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
self.best = max(self.best, node.val + left_gain + right_gain)
return node.val + left_gain + right_gain   # illegal: both branches up
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
self.best = max(self.best, node.val + left_gain + right_gain)
return node.val + max(left_gain, right_gain)  # one branch up

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Initializing the answer to zero
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The path must contain at least one node and all values can be negative, so the true answer may be negative. Starting at 0 returns 0 for a tree like [-3], which is wrong.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
private int best = 0;            // wrong for all-negative trees
// ... best = Math.max(best, node.val + leftGain + rightGain);
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
private int best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;  // any real path sum can win
// ... best = Math.max(best, node.val + leftGain + rightGain);

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not clamping negative gains
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If a child's best downward gain is negative, including it only lowers the sum. Clamping with max(0, gain) lets the algorithm skip that branch entirely.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
left_gain = gain(node.left)        # may be negative and dragged in
right_gain = gain(node.right)
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
left_gain = max(gain(node.left), 0)   # skip harmful branches
right_gain = max(gain(node.right), 0)

patternNote: Post-order DFS that returns a partial (single-branch) value while recording a complete (split) value globally. Reach for it whenever the answer can bend at a node but the value you hand a parent must stay a straight chain. Same engine as Diameter of Binary Tree, Longest Univalue Path, and Maximum Sum BST.
